outcome: No human-checked resolution of the unforced smooth-data question has been published since 26 January 2024. Two Lean-formalised announcements of 7 and 8 September 2026 bear on it directly: Buckmaster and Alpöge's finite-time blow-up for 3D Euler with smooth forcing (a forced, analogue case), and OpenAI's finite-time blow-up for unforced 3D Euler from smooth compactly supported data on R^3, whose statement fidelity has not been checked by humans and whose credit is disputed. Restricted-class results (Shkoller, March 2026; Chen, May 2026; Chen–Hou, computer-assisted, with arXiv versions from 2022–23 and a PNAS record in 2025), numerical candidates (Gómez-Serrano et al., September 2025; Ganeshram–Duruisseaux–Anandkumar, September 2026), and a conflicting claim of global existence (Ri, January 2026) also bear on it.
problem_asks: The bullet reads only 'Regularity of solutions of Euler equations', linking to 'Euler equations (fluid dynamics)'. I took the standard open question for the incompressible Euler equations as the reading. Parts: (i) for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations with no forcing and no viscosity, starting from smooth initial data (smooth, finite-energy, decaying or compactly supported, on R^3 in the usual formulation), does the solution stay smooth for all time, or can it develop a singularity in finite time, meaning blow-up of the velocity gradient or the vorticity? (ii) The same question for smooth data on a bounded domain or on the torus, if the bullet is read to include it; the bullet does not enumerate it. (iii) The two-dimensional incompressible case is classically known to be globally regular, so it is not part of the open question. Scope flag: the bullet does not say incompressible or compressible, or 2D or 3D, so a compressible reading (shock formation and vorticity blow-up) is possible; I did not research it beyond noting it (see incomplete and competing_reading).

disputes.summary: Credit and method provenance for the September 2026 Euler and Navier–Stokes claims. Buckmaster (with Alpöge) alleges that OpenAI learned of their unpublished work about a week before the 8 Sep announcement and pursued the same method, and that OpenAI proposed a joint paper that would have dropped Alpöge because he works at Anthropic. OpenAI says its effort began around 1 Sep after an unattributed rumour and that it contacted the pair on 6 Sep proposing a concurrent release crediting their Euler priority. OpenAI's math lead Sébastien Bubeck denies using the pair's prompts or proofs and says the NS proof was developed over the weekend. OpenAI (per Wikipedia and Unite) says it recognises the Buckmaster–Alpöge priority for the forced Euler result. The dispute is ongoing as of late September and early October 2026.

Ri (arXiv 2601.15685, Jan 2026) claims global existence of Euler solutions from H^s data with s≥−1+d/2 (d≥3), by vanishing viscosity. OpenAI (Sep 2026) claims finite-time blow-up of unforced smooth compactly supported data on R^3. If the classes overlap, both cannot be right. This is an inference from the Ri abstract's stated class, which I did not verify from the full text; no referee or expert has addressed the conflict.

Zhang (2025, not located) objects to the Chen–Hou computer-assisted Hou–Luo analysis: that his nonexistence results for self-similar profiles of axisymmetric Euler bear on Hou–Luo, and that a nonlocal error discrepancy undermines the stability estimates. Chen and Hou (arXiv 2608.15174, 15 Aug 2026) reply that the discrepancy compares the raw nonlocal Poisson error with the profile residual error, which are different quantities. No published reply from Zhang and no referee verdict found.

Press coverage conflates forced and unforced Euler results (e.g. the Scientific American and Quanta pieces describe the Buckmaster–Alpöge result and the OpenAI result without consistent labels), and the figures for the Euler agent run differ across relays (nearly 100 agents for about 50 hours versus 1,000 agents in one aggregator). The OpenAI primary page (403) and the 57-page OpenAI Euler manuscript (not decodable) could not be read to settle these. The record uses the forced/unforced labels from the authors' repositories and the README where available.

Fields Medallists' open letter, 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics' (11 Sep 2026; 25 signatories per a secondary report, including Tao). It objects to rushed announcements without writeups and to attribution, and does not call any proof wrong. It names neither OpenAI nor Anthropic and does not name a result. Recorded as commentary, not verification.

summary: Since 26 January 2024 the bullet's question (incompressible Euler, unforced, smooth data, regularity or finite-time blow-up) has no result that a human expert has checked in writing and published; the two decisive claims are both announcements from September 2026 with Lean formalisations and no refereed review. OpenAI (8 Sep 2026) claims finite-time blow-up for unforced 3D Euler from smooth compactly supported data on R^3; the README at github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler describes it, a Zenodo rebuild (17 Sep 2026) reports zero sorryAx and an Euler replay exit 0, and Stanford Tech Review counted placeholder sorry only in statement files; Quanta says the human check of the Lean statement is still pending. I could not read the 57-page OpenAI manuscript or the OpenAI page (HTTP 403), so the AI-involvement sentences are relayed from Unite, Quanta and RPI. Buckmaster and Alpöge (7 Sep 2026, NYU-hosted; Lean-verified per their repository) prove blow-up for 3D Euler with smooth space-time forcing from smooth axisymmetric data with swirl; that is the forced analogue, and Tao calls it 'a remarkable achievement' while saying he has not yet digested it. Their AI involvement is strong: Tao's post says 'the arguments here are heavily AI-assisted', Quanta reports Buckmaster's 'most horrendous' remark, and the Euler README (relayed) credits Claude with the Lean code under Alpöge's direction; none of this is quoted from the authors' own text, which could not be decoded. Restricted-class results point the same way without AI: Shkoller (11 Mar 2026, 159 pp., unpublished; informally endorsed by Scott Armstrong) proves Type-I blow-up for axisymmetric no-swirl Euler with C^{1,α} data, α<1/3, and Chen (May 2026) gives asymptotically self-similar blow-up in the same class; Chen and Hou's computer-assisted axisymmetric-with-boundary result (arXiv 2022/2023; PNAS 2025) is the most journal-checked restricted result, and its objection from Zhang is answered by the authors in August 2026. Numerical candidates include the DeepMind-linked unstable-singularity paper (Gómez-Serrano et al., 17 Sep 2025; boundary, axisymmetric; no proof) and Ganeshram–Duruisseaux–Anandkumar (9 Sep 2026; PINN-found approximate profile on R^3 with blow-up rate 0.5, certified by splines, with a conditional stability framework in 2609.10860); the authors of 2609.10867 state that LLMs played only a limited supporting role in their own work, while stating that the PINN framework, ansatz and optimisation were their own (2609.10867, not 2609.10860, carries that statement). Ri (22 Jan 2026, single author, unreviewed) claims global existence for Euler from H^s data, which would conflict with OpenAI's blow-up if the classes overlap; I have not resolved which, if either, is in error. Pre-window background: Elgindi (2019/2021, C^{1,α} on R^3, axisymmetric no-swirl), Chen–Hou (2019/2021, CMP, C^{1,α} with boundary), Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa–Zheng (Aug 2023, unforced 3D Euler on R^3 from data smooth away from one point, published Ann. PDE 2025), and Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa (Sep 2023, forced, non-axisymmetric), none of which is the smooth-data unforced question. Close calls: (a) whether the bullet means incompressible 3D unforced smooth data, which I assumed because the bullet is only a title; (b) whether OpenAI's claim counts before a human checks the Lean statement; (c) whether a PINN is an 'AI system' (I list it as a method class, as the sources do not name a product); (d) whether the forced Buckmaster–Alpöge result counts as the same question (I treat it as an analogue).
competing_reading: Read strictly as the unforced whole-space smooth-data question, the OpenAI claim settles the question in the blow-up direction if its Lean statement matches; the question then has a formal answer that no human has checked against the intended statement. A stricter reader treats it as unsettled: no referee, a human statement audit is outstanding, and Ri's claim points the other way. A broader reader takes 'regularity of solutions of Euler equations' to include forced variants and compressible Euler (shock formation, vorticity blow-up in 2024–2026 papers such as arXiv 2408.04319 and 2407.06455, which I saw in search results but did not open), in which case the Buckmaster–Alpöge forced result and several 2024–2026 compressible results count and the answer changes. A reader who weighs only peer-reviewed or long-checked results would count only the Chen–Hou PNAS paper (restricted) and find the general question open.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A human audit of the Lean statements in openai/NavierStokesAndEuler (Euler.lean and ComparatorChallenges) showing the formal statement is the unforced whole-space Euler blow-up, followed by refereed publication of the OpenAI Euler manuscript. (2) A written verification by a named PDE specialist of the Buckmaster–Alpöge Euler argument, and the actual NYU-hosted euler.pdf text (currently undecoded). (3) An error report or confirmation for Ri (arXiv 2601.15685), to resolve the conflict with the OpenAI class. (4) For the Ganeshram–Duruisseaux–Anandkumar line: completed certification of the profile constants and the continuation argument (2609.10860). (5) Zhang's 2025 nonexistence paper, to judge the Chen–Hou objection. (6) For the bullet's scope: the judging pass's decision on whether unforced 3D smooth data is the intended question, and whether compressible results count.

event.what_happened: OpenAI, announcement of 8 Sep 2026: 'Finite time blowup for the Euler equation' (57-page manuscript, cdn.openai.com PDF, not decodable through the fetch tool) with a Lean 4 formalisation in github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler (Apache-2.0). Per the README: constructs smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial velocity on R^3 whose unforced solution develops a finite-time singularity, with T* in (0, ∞); the velocity's C^1 norm is unbounded near T* and the time integral of the vorticity's L∞ norm diverges. OpenAI describes it as a 'preliminary step' before the Navier–Stokes run: agents 'resolved the regularity problem for the Euler equations in the unforced variant where no external force is applied' (relayed). Credit: OpenAI says it recognises Alpöge and Buckmaster's priority for the forced Euler result. Read: README (GitHub), relays via Unite, Quanta, Kingy, RPI, Stanford Tech Review and the Zenodo audit. The OpenAI page itself returned HTTP 403.

judgement.why: The bullet is a bare title; I read it, as the record does, as the standard question for 3D incompressible unforced Euler from smooth data on R^3. On that reading the OpenAI unforced claim (smooth compactly supported data on R^3, finite-time blow-up) answers the question: scope whole, verification unreviewed because a sorry-free Lean replay is not a human reading and statement fidelity is still pending (F7). It is doubtful but not set aside, since no error has been identified. The AI produced the proof by OpenAI's account, so its role is generated. Everything in non-smooth data classes (Elgindi, CMZ-Zheng, Shkoller, Chen), forced settings (Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa, Buckmaster–Alpöge, OpenAI NS), other equations and other dimensions is a variant. Chen–Hou smooth data with boundary is a case: it is axisymmetric in a bounded domain, it is pre-snapshot, and PNAS has accepted it. Numerical profiles, conditional frameworks and constraints are none. Ri's global-existence claim would be whole if true, but it is not_credible: one author, a claim that also covers Navier–Stokes, no uptake, and contradicted by later work.
judgement.doubts: Scope rests on reading the vague bullet as R^3 unforced smooth data. If the torus and bounded-domain versions count as separate parts, the OpenAI event is a case, not whole. Compressible Euler was not researched. PINN events marked assisted are moot because they score none. The OpenAI claim's theorem text comes only from the README and relays.
